Affiliation:: Department of Mathematics, University of Oklahoma
Application Areas: Calculating volumes of orbit spaces or leaf spaces
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Generalizing Homogeneous Settings: Extends classical theorems from rigid group actions (homogeneous spaces) to more flexible settings like singular Riemannian foliations and submetries (e.g. Generalizes Kostant's Convexity Theorem, traditionally for polar representations, to the broader context of arbitrary submetries).

Connecting Geometry and Algebra: Establishes a direct correspondence between geometric properties and algebraic structures, translating problems between the two fields (e.g., Establishes a one-to-one correspondence between infinitesimal manifold submetries (geometry) and Laplacian algebras (algebra)).

Unifying Geometric Frameworks: Develops abstract concepts to unify seemingly disparate geometric objects, like different representations or foliations, under a single theoretical structure (e.g., Introduces 'fat sections' as a concept to generalize and unify polar representations, representations of non-trivial copolarity, and isoparametric foliations).

Applying Analysis to Geometry: Applies powerful analytic techniques (spectral theory, heat kernels, asymptotic estimates) to solve fundamental problems in geometry, such as calculating volumes (e.g., Uses Hörmander's estimate, heat kernels, and Tauberian theorems to prove a Weyl's law for foliations, linking the analytic spectrum to the geometric volume of the leaf space).
Summary Description: Dr. Ricardo A. E. Mendes specializes in Differential Geometry and Invariant Theory, focusing on the connections between Riemannian geometry, representation theory, and convex algebraic geometry. His research generalizes classical concepts from group actions to the broader settings of singular Riemannian foliations and submetries. He investigates relationships between geometric invariants (like diameter and focal radius), spectral properties (like Weyl's law for foliations), and the algebraic structure of "Laplacian algebras," which generalize invariant polynomials. A significant part of his work involves creating unifying frameworks, such as introducing "fat sections" to generalize Kostant's Convexity Theorem and applying analytic techniques (like heat kernels) to geometric problems. He also solves problems in invariant theory and analyzes invariant spectrahedra.
